common_name: Duchesse d'Angoulême Pear (Enormous Knobby French Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Duchesse d'Angoulême is a French heirloom from the early 1800s grown for one of the largest, most irregularly knobby and lopsided fruit shapes of any common pear, a genuinely striking apple-defying form that can make individual pears weigh over a pound. Beneath the rough, uneven skin, the flesh is buttery, juicy, and richly flavored, excellent for fresh eating once fully ripe and equally good poached or baked given its substantial size. The tree is a reliable, moderately vigorous producer; harvest while still firm and green, since like most European pears it should be picked underripe and finished ripening indoors at room temperature for the best texture and flavor.

common_name: Beurré Giffard Pear (Early-Ripening French Summer Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Beurré Giffard is a French heirloom from the 1820s prized for ripening remarkably early, among the very first quality European pears of the summer, well ahead of the classic fall and winter storage pears most gardeners grow. The medium, greenish-yellow fruit blushed with red has soft, juicy, melting, richly flavored flesh in the classic 'buttery' (beurré) style, but the tradeoff for its buttery texture and early ripening is a very short window of peak quality — the fruit must be picked at just the right moment and eaten promptly, since it goes from underripe to overripe quickly with little margin. For gardeners willing to watch the crop closely, it rewards with some of the season's first fresh pears.

Flemish Beauty originated in Belgium around 1810 and became historically important in North American pear growing for its outstanding cold hardiness, allowing pear cultivation in regions too harsh for many other European varieties. The large, golden-yellow fruit blushed with russet has sweet, aromatic, juicy flesh with real depth of flavor when picked and ripened properly. The tree's biggest weakness is susceptibility to fire blight and pear scab, which can be a real challenge in humid, disease-prone climates, so it benefits from good air circulation and, where scab pressure is high, a basic fungicide program. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature for the best texture.

common_name: Louise Bonne Pear (Louise Bonne of Jersey, Reliable French Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Louise Bonne, widely known in England as Louise Bonne of Jersey, is a French heirloom dating to the 1780s that became one of the most reliably productive and widely planted pears of the 19th century, valued for its dependable, heavy annual bearing as much as its fruit quality. The medium, greenish-yellow pear blushed with brownish-red has juicy, sweet, melting flesh with a good, well-balanced flavor, excellent for fresh eating and reasonably good for canning as well. The vigorous, precocious tree tends to bear young and heavily, sometimes needing fruit thinning to avoid limb breakage or biennial bearing. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature for the best eating quality.

common_name: Harrow Delight Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Early Canadian Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred for strong fire blight resistance, making it a good choice for humid climates where that disease is a serious threat, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Harrow Delight was bred at the Harrow research station in Ontario, Canada, specifically for strong resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that is the single greatest threat to pear growing in warm, humid climates and can kill susceptible trees outright in a bad year. The medium, yellow fruit blushed with red ripens early in the season, ahead of many other pears, with sweet, juicy, smooth-textured flesh good for fresh eating. Its combination of disease resistance and early ripening has made it a practical, low-risk recommendation for home orchardists in the humid South and elsewhere where fire blight makes growing more susceptible heirloom pear varieties a genuine gamble. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature.
